cards.title: morning
cards.meaning: The early part of the day, before the afternoon.
cards.example: I read in the morning.
cards.conversation:
A: Good morning, Sam.
B: Good morning, Mia.
cards.exercise: Complete: I read in the ____.
cards.answer: morning
cards.synonymNote: These phrases explain the time of day.
cards.notes: Say in the morning. Use at with a time: at seven.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for morning: sun.

cards.title: choose
cards.meaning: To pick the thing you want from two or more things.
cards.example: I choose a blue cup.
cards.conversation:
A: Which cup do you choose?
B: I choose the blue one.
cards.exercise: Complete: I ____ a blue cup.
cards.answer: choose
cards.synonymNote: Pick is common in everyday speech.
cards.notes: Say choose a cup or choose a book. The past form is chose.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for choose: magnifier.

cards.title: wake up
cards.meaning: To stop sleeping.
cards.example: I wake up at seven.
cards.conversation:
A: When do you wake up?
B: At seven.
cards.exercise: Complete: I wake ____ at seven.
cards.answer: up
cards.notes: Say I wake up at seven. To wake another person, say wake them up.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for wake up: path.

cards.title: put on
cards.meaning: To place clothes or shoes on your body.
cards.example: I put on my shoes.
cards.conversation:
A: Are you ready?
B: Yes. I will put on my shoes.
cards.exercise: Complete: I put ____ my shoes.
cards.answer: on
cards.notes: Say put on your shoes or put your shoes on. With them, say put them on.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for put on: path.

cards.title: take your time
cards.meaning: A friendly way to tell someone that they do not need to hurry.
cards.example: Take your time. We can wait.
cards.conversation:
A: I need two minutes.
B: Take your time.
cards.exercise: Tell a friend they do not need to hurry.
cards.answer: Take your time.
cards.notes: Say Take your time when you can wait for another person.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for take your time: clock.

cards.title: so far, so good
cards.meaning: Everything is going well up to now.
cards.example: My morning? So far, so good.
cards.conversation:
A: How is your day?
B: So far, so good.
cards.exercise: Complete: So far, so ____.
cards.answer: good
cards.notes: Use this short expression when someone asks how something is going.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for so far, so good: compass.

cards.title: I have time for one small thing.
cards.meaning: I can use a little time to do one simple activity.
cards.example: I have time for one small thing. I can read a page.
cards.conversation:
A: Do you have time to read?
B: Yes, I have time for one page.
cards.exercise: Complete: I have time ____ one small thing.
cards.answer: for
cards.notes: Use have time for + a thing: I have time for a book. Use have time to + a verb: I have time to read.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for I have time for one small thing.: clock.

cards.title: A new day starts with one small step.
cards.meaning: You can begin a new day by doing one simple thing.
cards.example: I open my book. A new day starts with one small step.
cards.conversation:
A: This book is long.
B: Start with one page.
cards.exercise: Write one small thing you do in the morning.
cards.answer: I open the window.
cards.notes: This is an original practice sentence. A small step can mean a small action.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for A new day starts with one small step.: light.

cards.title: At + a time
cards.meaning: Use at before a clock time.
cards.example: I wake up at seven.
cards.conversation:
A: When do you have breakfast?
B: At eight.
cards.exercise: Choose: I wake up (at / on) seven.
cards.answer: at
cards.notes: Say at seven or at eight thirty. Say in the morning for a part of the day.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for At + a time: clock.

cards.title: How is your morning?
cards.meaning: A friendly question about someone's morning.
cards.example: How is your morning?
cards.conversation:
A: How is your morning?
B: Good, thank you. How about you?
cards.exercise: Reply and ask the question back.
cards.answer: Good, thank you. How about you?
cards.notes: You can answer Good, thank you and then ask How about you?
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for How is your morning?: sun.

cards.title: One quiet morning
cards.meaning: A short story about simple things to do in the morning.
paragraphs: A quiet morning helps me start my day. I have a good breakfast and time for my book.
First, I eat breakfast at seven. I choose bread and eggs. I drink some water too. The food is good.
Next, I read a page in my book. I sit by the window. I have time for one small thing I like.
Breakfast and a book make my morning nice. I feel good and I am ready for my day.
cards.exercise: What two things make the writer’s morning nice?
cards.answer: Breakfast and reading a book make the writer’s morning nice.
cards.structure: Main idea: a nice morning. Reason 1: breakfast. Reason 2: a book. End: put the two reasons together.

highlights.text: I have time for one small thing

cards.notes: Follow the main idea through two supported points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for One quiet morning: sun.

A1.source: James Real demonstration edition; original card format, level-specific English content.

cards.title: habit
cards.meaning: Something you do often, sometimes without thinking about it.
cards.example: Reading after breakfast is a new habit for me.
cards.conversation:
A: Do you read every day?
B: Yes. It is a useful habit.
cards.exercise: Complete: Reading each morning is a new ____.
cards.answer: habit
cards.synonymNote: A habit often happens without much thought.
cards.notes: A habit can be good or bad. Use a habit of + -ing: a habit of reading before bed.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for habit: magnifier.

cards.title: notice
cards.meaning: To see or become aware of something.
cards.example: I notice the flowers on my way to work.
cards.conversation:
A: Did you notice the new shop?
B: Yes. It is next to the park.
cards.exercise: Complete: I ____ the flowers on my way to work.
cards.answer: notice
cards.synonymNote: Notice adds the idea that something reaches your attention.
cards.notes: Use notice + a thing: notice a bird. Use notice that + a sentence: notice that it is raining.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for notice: magnifier.

cards.title: slow down
cards.meaning: To move or do something more slowly.
cards.example: I slow down when I walk through the park.
cards.conversation:
A: You are walking very fast.
B: You’re right. Let’s slow down.
cards.exercise: Complete: Let’s slow ____ and look around.
cards.answer: down
cards.notes: Use it when the speed is too fast: Please slow down. You can also slow something down.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for slow down: path.

cards.title: make time for
cards.meaning: To arrange your day so that you can do something.
cards.example: I make time for a short walk after lunch.
cards.conversation:
A: How do you find time to read?
B: I make time for it after breakfast.
cards.exercise: Complete: I make time ____ a short walk.
cards.answer: for
cards.notes: Use make time for + a noun or -ing: make time for reading. Use make time to read before a verb.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for make time for: clock.

cards.title: step by step
cards.meaning: By doing one small part and then the next.
cards.example: I am learning to cook, step by step.
cards.conversation:
A: This recipe looks difficult.
B: We can follow it step by step.
cards.exercise: Complete: We can learn it step by ____.
cards.answer: step
cards.notes: Use it to describe steady progress: We learn step by step.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for step by step: compass.

cards.title: less is more
cards.meaning: A saying that a simple choice can sometimes be better than a complicated one.
cards.example: I keep only three things on my desk. Less is more.
cards.conversation:
A: Your desk looks simple.
B: Yes. For me, less is more.
cards.exercise: What does “less is more” suggest here?
cards.answer: A simpler desk works better for this person.
cards.notes: It does not mean that less is always better. Use it when keeping things simple helps.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for less is more: compass.

cards.title: I am trying to do one thing at a time.
cards.meaning: A way to say that you are practising doing one task before starting another.
cards.example: I am trying to do one thing at a time.
cards.conversation:
A: Are you checking your phone while reading?
B: No. I am trying to do one thing at a time.
cards.exercise: Complete: I am trying to do one thing ____ a time.
cards.answer: at
cards.notes: Try to + a verb describes an effort. One thing at a time means doing tasks separately.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for I am trying to do one thing at a time.: clock.

cards.title: Small changes can make an ordinary day feel new.
cards.meaning: A little difference in your routine can make the day feel fresh.
cards.example: I take a different path to the park. Small changes can make an ordinary day feel new.
cards.conversation:
A: Did you do anything different today?
B: I had breakfast by the window.
cards.exercise: Describe one small change to your day.
cards.answer: I can walk to a different café.
cards.notes: This is an original practice reflection. Ordinary means usual, rather than special.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for Small changes can make an ordinary day feel new.: path.

cards.title: Adverbs of frequency
cards.meaning: Words such as always, usually, often, sometimes, and never show how often something happens.
cards.example: I usually read after breakfast. I am often home before six.
cards.conversation:
A: Do you always walk to work?
B: No. I sometimes take the bus.
cards.exercise: Put in order: usually / I / after lunch / walk.
cards.answer: I usually walk after lunch.
cards.notes: They usually go before a main verb: I often read. They go after be: I am usually ready.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for Adverbs of frequency: notebook.

cards.title: What do you like to do before work?
cards.meaning: A friendly question about activities someone enjoys before starting work.
cards.example: What do you like to do before work?
cards.conversation:
A: What do you like to do before work?
B: I like to read for ten minutes. What about you?
cards.exercise: Give a short answer and ask the question back.
cards.answer: I like to have a quiet breakfast. What about you?
cards.notes: Use like to + a verb or like + -ing. Ask about one activity in the person's reply.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for What do you like to do before work?: desk.

cards.title: Ten minutes for myself
cards.meaning: How ten quiet minutes can make a busy morning feel different.
paragraphs: Ten quiet minutes can make a busy morning better. I use this time to enjoy breakfast and read a little. These two small habits help me start the day calmly.
First, a slow breakfast helps me notice the world around me. I usually leave my phone on the shelf for ten minutes. I sit by the window and eat slowly. Sometimes I watch birds in the tree outside.
Second, a little reading gives me time for something I enjoy. I read one or two pages after breakfast. I do not need to finish a whole chapter. I build this habit step by step.
Eating slowly and reading a little make my mornings more enjoyable. My day is still busy, but I have made time for myself. I want to keep these simple habits.
cards.exercise: Where does the writer leave the phone, and for how long?
cards.answer: The writer leaves the phone on the shelf for ten minutes.
cards.structure: Introduce two helpful habits. Give a breakfast example and a reading example in separate paragraphs. Finish by restating their shared benefit.
cards.notes: Follow the main idea through two supported points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for Ten minutes for myself: book.

A2.source: James Real demonstration edition; original card format, level-specific English content.

cards.title: routine
cards.meaning: The usual order or way in which you do regular activities.
cards.example: A simple evening routine helps me remember what I need for tomorrow.
cards.conversation:
A: Has your routine changed?
B: Yes. I pack my bag in the evening now.
cards.exercise: Complete: Packing my bag is part of my evening ____.
cards.answer: routine
cards.synonymNote: A routine can include several habits; a schedule focuses on their timing.
cards.notes: A morning routine describes your normal morning activities. Routine can be a noun or an adjective; here it is a noun.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for routine: clock.

cards.title: priority
cards.meaning: Something you think is more important than other things and should receive attention first.
cards.example: Spending time with my family is a priority this week.
cards.conversation:
A: What is your main priority today?
B: Finishing the letter I promised to write.
cards.exercise: Name one priority for your day.
cards.answer: My priority is to finish my homework.
cards.synonymNote: A priority receives attention before less important matters.
cards.notes: Say a priority or your main priority. Priorities is the plural form.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for priority: calendar.

cards.title: cut back on
cards.meaning: To reduce the amount of something you use or do.
cards.example: I want to cut back on checking my phone during dinner.
cards.conversation:
A: Are you giving up your phone?
B: No. I am just cutting back on using it at dinner.
cards.exercise: Complete: I want to cut back ____ screen time at dinner.
cards.answer: on
cards.notes: Use cut back on + a noun or -ing: cut back on screen time or on checking messages.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for cut back on: path.

cards.title: stick to
cards.meaning: To continue following a plan, decision, or habit.
cards.example: It is easier to stick to a plan when it is realistic.
cards.conversation:
A: How is your new reading plan?
B: I can stick to ten minutes a day.
cards.exercise: Complete: I can stick ____ a simple plan.
cards.answer: to
cards.notes: Use stick to + a noun or -ing: stick to a plan. The past form is stuck to.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for stick to: path.

cards.title: a fresh start
cards.meaning: A new beginning, especially after difficulties or an unsatisfactory experience.
cards.example: Monday felt like a fresh start after I organised my desk.
cards.conversation:
A: Why did you change your workspace?
B: I wanted a fresh start.
cards.exercise: Complete: I wanted a ____ start.
cards.answer: fresh
cards.notes: Say make a fresh start. Fresh suggests a new opportunity, not that earlier experience disappears.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for a fresh start: basket.

cards.title: break the ice
cards.meaning: To make people feel more relaxed at the start of a conversation or meeting.
cards.example: Asking about the book on her desk helped break the ice.
cards.conversation:
A: How did you start talking to your new neighbour?
B: I asked about her dog to break the ice.
cards.exercise: Suggest one question that could break the ice.
cards.answer: Have you lived in this neighbourhood long?
cards.notes: An easy, friendly question can break the ice. Avoid personal questions that could make someone uncomfortable.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for break the ice: compass.

cards.title: I would rather make a small change that I can keep.
cards.meaning: A way to express a preference for a manageable change that can continue over time.
cards.example: I would rather make a small change that I can keep.
cards.conversation:
A: Why not change your whole schedule?
B: I would rather make a small change that I can keep.
cards.exercise: Complete: I would rather ____ one useful habit.
cards.answer: build
cards.notes: Use would rather + the base verb, without to: I would rather start small.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for I would rather make a small change that I can keep.: path.

cards.title: The best routine leaves room for real life.
cards.meaning: A useful routine allows for the unexpected events and needs of daily life.
cards.example: Plans sometimes change. The best routine leaves room for real life.
cards.conversation:
A: I missed my walk because a friend visited.
B: You can return to your routine tomorrow.
cards.exercise: Name one reason a routine may need to change.
cards.answer: A friend may need help unexpectedly.
cards.notes: This is an original practice reflection. Leave room for means allow space or flexibility, not only physical room.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for The best routine leaves room for real life.: room.

cards.title: Used to + verb
cards.meaning: Use used to + a verb for a past habit or state that is no longer true.
cards.example: I used to check my phone during breakfast, but now I read.
cards.conversation:
A: Did you always walk to the station?
B: No. I used to take the bus.
cards.exercise: Complete: I ____ to leave everything until the morning.
cards.answer: used
cards.notes: Do not confuse it with be used to + -ing, which means be familiar with something.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for Used to + verb: notebook.

cards.title: Have you tried anything new lately?
cards.meaning: A friendly question about recent experiences or activities.
cards.example: Have you tried anything new lately?
cards.conversation:
A: Have you tried anything new lately?
B: I have started writing a short note each evening.
cards.exercise: Ask one follow-up about the new activity.
cards.answer: What do you enjoy about writing those notes?
cards.notes: The present perfect links recent experience to now. Lately usually means during the recent past.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for Have you tried anything new lately?: dialogue.

cards.title: A routine that fits
cards.meaning: Why a small, realistic routine can be easier to keep than an ambitious plan.
paragraphs: A useful routine should fit real life. I learned that choosing one realistic priority and returning after interruptions work better than making an ambitious plan I cannot keep.

First, a small priority is easier to act on. I used to plan several new activities every day, but I usually fell behind. Then I chose ten minutes of reading after dinner and put a book beside my chair. The clear, simple task was easier to remember.

Second, a flexible routine survives ordinary interruptions. Sometimes a visitor arrived or another task took longer than expected. Instead of giving up, I returned to reading the next evening. Missing one day did not mean abandoning the whole plan.

Realistic goals and flexible expectations helped reading become part of my day. A routine does not need to be impressive to be useful. It succeeds when it is simple enough to start and forgiving enough to continue.
cards.exercise: Why was the smaller plan easier to keep?
cards.answer: It focused on one realistic priority and allowed the writer to return to it after interruptions.
cards.structure: Claim: routines need realism and flexibility. Develop each reason with a personal example. Restate why both help a habit last.
cards.notes: Follow the main idea through two supported points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for A routine that fits: clock.

B1.source: James Real demonstration edition; original card format, level-specific English content.

cards.title: deliberate
cards.meaning: Done intentionally and with thought, rather than by accident.
cards.example: Leaving my phone in another room was a deliberate choice.
cards.conversation:
A: Did you forget your phone?
B: No. It was a deliberate decision to leave it behind.
A: Did leaving it behind make a difference?
B: Yes. I found it easier to stay with the conversation.
cards.exercise: Complete: It was a ____ choice, not an accident.
cards.answer: deliberate
cards.synonymNote: Intentional means not accidental; considered also suggests careful thought.
cards.notes: Here deliberate is an adjective. Its final syllable is weak; the verb deliberate has a different pronunciation and means consider carefully.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for deliberate: magnifier.

cards.title: distraction
cards.meaning: Something that takes your attention away from what you are doing.
cards.example: Even a quiet notification can become a distraction.
cards.conversation:
A: Why did you silence your notifications?
B: They were a distraction while I was writing.
A: Could you check them after you finish?
B: That is the plan. I do not need to respond immediately.
cards.exercise: Name one possible distraction while studying.
cards.answer: A phone notification can be a distraction.
cards.synonymNote: An interruption stops an activity; a distraction may only take attention away.
cards.notes: Use a distraction from an activity. In this context it interrupts concentration, though a distraction can sometimes be welcome.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for distraction: magnifier.

cards.title: set aside
cards.meaning: To reserve time, money, or another resource for a particular purpose.
cards.example: I set aside twenty minutes to read without interruptions.
cards.conversation:
A: When do you work on your sketchbook?
B: I set aside some time on Sunday afternoons.
A: Does that time stay free every week?
B: Usually, though I move it when something important comes up.
cards.exercise: Complete: I set ____ twenty minutes to read.
cards.answer: aside
cards.notes: Set aside time for reading or set time aside. With a pronoun, say set it aside.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for set aside: path.

cards.title: get around to
cards.meaning: To finally find the time to do something you intended to do.
cards.example: I finally got around to organising my photographs.
cards.conversation:
A: Did you sort out your photos?
B: Yes. I got around to it last weekend.
A: What helped you finally begin?
B: I chose a small group of photos instead of the entire collection.
cards.exercise: Complete: I got around to ____ my photographs. (organise)
cards.answer: organising
cards.notes: To is a preposition here, so use a noun or -ing: get around to organising the photos.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for get around to: path.

cards.title: spread yourself too thin
cards.meaning: To take on so many activities that you cannot give each enough time or attention.
cards.example: Taking on four new activities left me spread too thin.
cards.conversation:
A: Why did you leave one club?
B: I was spreading myself too thin.
A: Has having fewer commitments helped?
B: Yes. I can give more attention to the activities I kept.
cards.exercise: What practical problem does this expression describe?
cards.answer: Trying to do so much that you cannot give each activity enough attention.
cards.notes: The expression is informal and often warns about overcommitment. Change yourself to match the subject: I spread myself too thin.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for spread yourself too thin: compass.

cards.title: a change of pace
cards.meaning: An activity or rhythm that is pleasantly different from your usual one.
cards.example: An afternoon in the garden was a welcome change of pace.
cards.conversation:
A: How was the pottery class?
B: It was a lovely change of pace after a busy week.
A: Would you like to try it again?
B: Definitely. Working with my hands felt refreshing.
cards.exercise: Describe a change of pace you would enjoy.
cards.answer: A quiet afternoon of drawing would be a welcome change of pace.
cards.notes: A change of pace can be slower or faster. The phrase highlights variety, not necessarily relaxation.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for a change of pace: path.

cards.title: I want my schedule to reflect what matters to me.
cards.meaning: A way to say that your use of time should show your personal values.
cards.example: I want my schedule to reflect what matters to me, even in small ways.
cards.conversation:
A: Why did you reserve Friday evenings?
B: I want my schedule to reflect what matters to me.
A: What will you use those evenings for?
B: Spending time with my family and reading without rushing.
cards.exercise: Paraphrase “reflect what matters to me”.
cards.answer: Show what I consider important.
cards.notes: Reflect here means express or represent. What matters to me is a noun clause meaning what I consider important.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for I want my schedule to reflect what matters to me.: notebook.

cards.title: Attention gives ordinary moments their texture.
cards.meaning: Paying attention can reveal the richness and detail of everyday experiences.
cards.example: Listening closely, I noticed the pauses in my friend’s story. Attention gives ordinary moments their texture.
cards.conversation:
A: The walk looked ordinary.
B: It felt different when I paid attention to the sounds.
A: What did you notice first?
B: Birdsong that I normally missed while checking my phone.
cards.exercise: What does “texture” mean in this reflection?
cards.answer: The richness and detail of an experience.
cards.notes: This is an original practice reflection. Texture is metaphorical; it refers to felt qualities, not only a physical surface.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for Attention gives ordinary moments their texture.: magnifier.

cards.title: Present perfect continuous
cards.meaning: Use have or has been + -ing for an activity continuing from the past to now, or a recent activity with a present result.
cards.example: I have been trying to leave more space between appointments.
cards.conversation:
A: Why do your afternoons feel different?
B: I have been scheduling fewer meetings.
A: Has the change helped?
B: Yes. I have more time to finish one task before starting another.
cards.exercise: Complete: She has been ____ more time for drawing. (make)
cards.answer: making
cards.notes: I have been reading focuses on the activity. I have read the book often presents it as completed. Avoid the continuous with most stative verbs.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for Present perfect continuous: notebook.

cards.title: What has been a welcome change of pace for you?
cards.meaning: A question inviting someone to describe a recent activity that felt different and welcome.
cards.example: What has been a welcome change of pace for you recently?
cards.conversation:
A: What has been a welcome change of pace for you?
B: Taking a beginner’s pottery class. It feels good to make something slowly.
A: Is the pace different from your usual work?
B: Very different. I have to pay attention to the material itself.
cards.exercise: Ask a follow-up that explores the experience.
cards.answer: What do you enjoy most about working with clay?
cards.notes: The present perfect connects the experience to the present. Follow up on what made the change enjoyable.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for What has been a welcome change of pace for you?: path.

cards.title: Designing a day with breathing room
cards.meaning: How deliberate choices about time can leave more room for attention.
paragraphs: A meaningful schedule needs more than a full calendar. Protecting valued activities and leaving gaps between commitments can create the breathing room needed for sustained attention.

First, protecting one priority makes it easier to act on what matters. I made a deliberate adjustment by setting aside time to read before opening my messages. Some replies had to wait, but reading finally became part of my day rather than a postponed intention.

Second, small gaps prevent commitments from competing for every available minute. I began leaving a short break after meetings instead of scheduling another task immediately. That pause helped me recognise when I was spreading myself too thin and adjust the rest of the day.

Protected priorities and deliberate gaps both make attention more sustainable. Neither requires a completely empty calendar; each requires accepting limits. I now judge my schedule by the room it gives meaningful activities, as well as the tasks it contains.
cards.exercise: What two changes does the writer recommend, and what trade-off is involved?
cards.answer: Protect time for valued activities and leave gaps between commitments. This can mean delaying replies or fitting fewer tasks into the day.
cards.structure: Thesis: attention needs protected priorities and gaps. Explain each with a practical example. Conclude by acknowledging the trade-off.
cards.notes: Follow the main idea through two supported points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for Designing a day with breathing room: room.

B2.source: James Real demonstration edition; original card format, level-specific English content.

cards.title: intentionality
cards.meaning: The quality of acting with conscious purpose or a considered aim.
cards.example: Intentionality can be expressed through modest, repeatable choices.
cards.conversation:
A: Does every habit need a grand purpose?
B: No. Intentionality can be quiet and practical.
A: What makes an ordinary choice intentional?
B: Knowing why it matters and choosing it with that purpose in mind.
cards.exercise: Complete: Her choices showed care and ____.
cards.answer: intentionality
cards.synonymNote: These fit the everyday sense here, not every specialised use of intentionality.
cards.notes: Usually uncountable. In everyday discussion it concerns purposeful action; in philosophy the term also has a distinct technical sense.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for intentionality: magnifier.

cards.title: friction
cards.meaning: Resistance or difficulty that makes an action harder to begin or complete.
cards.example: Keeping materials within reach reduces the friction of getting started.
cards.conversation:
A: Why leave the sketchbook open?
B: It reduces the friction of beginning.
A: Does that remove the need for effort?
B: No, but it makes the first action less demanding.
cards.exercise: Give an example of reducing friction for reading.
cards.answer: Keeping a book beside your usual chair can reduce the friction of starting.
cards.synonymNote: These fit the figurative sense of obstacles to starting or continuing an activity.
cards.notes: This is a figurative use. Reducing friction means removing obstacles, not necessarily removing every effort involved in an activity.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for friction: magnifier.

cards.title: default to
cards.meaning: To adopt a familiar option automatically when no deliberate alternative is chosen.
cards.example: When I feel rushed, I default to checking messages.
cards.conversation:
A: Why did you open the app again?
B: I tend to default to it between tasks.
A: Would moving the app help?
B: It might create a pause in which I can choose more deliberately.
cards.exercise: Complete: Under pressure, I default ____ familiar routines.
cards.answer: to
cards.notes: Use default to + a noun or -ing. It can describe a useful standard choice or an unexamined habit, depending on context.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for default to: path.

cards.title: carve out
cards.meaning: To secure time, space, or an opportunity despite competing demands.
cards.example: She carved out a quiet hour for her writing.
cards.conversation:
A: How do you keep your creative work going?
B: I carve out a little time before the day becomes busy.
A: How do you protect that time?
B: I keep the commitment small enough to sustain.
cards.exercise: Rewrite using “carve out”: She made time for reflection.
cards.answer: She carved out time for reflection.
cards.notes: Carve out time for something suggests effort in protecting a limited resource. With a pronoun, say carve it out.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for carve out: path.

cards.title: go through the motions
cards.meaning: To perform an activity mechanically without real interest, commitment, or attention.
cards.example: I was attending every meeting but merely going through the motions.
cards.conversation:
A: Did you enjoy the activity?
B: Honestly, I was just going through the motions.
A: What would help you reconnect with it?
B: Remembering what interested me before it became another obligation.
cards.exercise: What is missing when someone goes through the motions?
cards.answer: Genuine attention, enthusiasm or engagement.
cards.notes: Usually critical or self-critical. The outward actions occur, but the speaker questions the engagement behind them.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for go through the motions: compass.

cards.title: lose sight of
cards.meaning: To stop keeping an important purpose or fact in mind.
cards.example: We can lose sight of enjoyment when every hobby becomes a target.
cards.conversation:
A: Why did you stop counting the pages you read?
B: I had lost sight of why I enjoyed reading.
A: What did you want to recover?
B: The pleasure of following an idea without counting progress.
cards.exercise: Complete: I had lost ____ of the original purpose.
cards.answer: sight
cards.notes: Use lose sight of + a noun or clause. Here it is metaphorical rather than a loss of physical vision.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for lose sight of: compass.

cards.title: The aim is to make the valued choice easier to repeat.
cards.meaning: A statement that the goal is to help someone repeat an action they already consider worthwhile.
cards.example: The aim is to make the valued choice easier to repeat, not to perfect every minute.
cards.conversation:
A: Why place your guitar beside the sofa?
B: The aim is to make the valued choice easier to repeat.
A: Does the arrangement work on difficult days?
B: It helps, but I also allow the routine to change.
cards.exercise: Explain this aim using a specific example.
cards.answer: Keeping art supplies ready makes it easier to choose drawing again.
cards.notes: Valued identifies the action's significance to the person. Easier to repeat concerns its conditions, not a demand for perfect consistency.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for The aim is to make the valued choice easier to repeat.: scales.

cards.title: What we make convenient quietly shapes what we become.
cards.meaning: The activities we make easy to access can gradually influence our habits and identity.
cards.example: A book within reach invited a different habit. What we make convenient quietly shapes what we become.
cards.conversation:
A: Did moving the phone really change anything?
B: It changed what I reached for first.
A: So convenience influences rather than determines behaviour?
B: Exactly. It changes the conditions in which choices are made.
cards.exercise: Does the reflection claim convenience determines every choice?
cards.answer: No. It suggests convenience influences repeated choices, without claiming it determines them all.
cards.notes: This is an original practice reflection. Shapes suggests influence, not complete determination; quietly points to changes that may go unnoticed.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for What we make convenient quietly shapes what we become.: light.

cards.title: What-cleft sentences
cards.meaning: A sentence pattern using a what-clause and be to focus attention on particular information.
cards.example: What I needed was a routine that allowed for interruptions.
cards.conversation:
A: Was stricter planning the solution?
B: No. What helped was making the first step smaller.
A: Why did that make a difference?
B: It replaced an intimidating goal with something I could begin.
cards.exercise: Emphasise “a little flexibility”: I needed a little flexibility.
cards.answer: What I needed was a little flexibility.
cards.notes: What I needed was flexibility. The focused element follows be. Maintain suitable tense and agreement rather than treating the pattern as a fixed slogan.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for What-cleft sentences: notebook.

cards.title: Which part of your routine feels most like a choice?
cards.meaning: A reflective question about which regular activity feels consciously chosen rather than automatic.
cards.example: Which part of your routine feels most like a choice?
cards.conversation:
A: Which part of your routine feels most like a choice?
B: Walking home by the river. I could take a faster route, but I enjoy the extra time.
A: What does the slower route give you?
B: A sense that the day includes something chosen for its own sake.
cards.exercise: Ask a follow-up about the value behind that choice.
cards.answer: What does that extra time by the river give you?
cards.notes: The phrase most like a choice invites interpretation. It does not imply that habits and choices are mutually exclusive.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for Which part of your routine feels most like a choice?: clock.

cards.title: Making room for what matters
cards.meaning: How environments and flexible routines can support activities we value.
paragraphs: Everyday change depends on more than willpower. Meaningful routines are more likely to last when environments reduce friction and expectations remain flexible enough to preserve the value of the activity itself.

Reducing friction makes a valued choice easier to begin. A notebook left open or reading materials prepared in advance removes a small but repeated obstacle. Someone who wants to write after dinner, for instance, can prepare a quiet space before the evening becomes crowded with other demands.

Flexible expectations protect the purpose behind the routine. A reader who treats a daily page target as compulsory may lose the pleasure that motivated the habit. Allowing a shorter session on a demanding day preserves engagement without making measurement the activity’s sole justification.

What I find useful is therefore a balance between supportive structure and permission to adapt. The former eases the first step; the latter preserves meaning when circumstances change. Intentionality works best when it supports ordinary life rather than demanding perfect predictability.
cards.exercise: What risk does the third paragraph identify?
cards.answer: Measuring and optimising an activity can displace the enjoyment or meaning that originally made it valuable.
cards.structure: Establish two conditions for lasting routines. Explain reduced friction and flexible expectations with distinct examples. Synthesize their complementary roles.
cards.notes: Follow the main idea through two supported points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for Making room for what matters: room.

C1.source: James Real demonstration edition; original card format, level-specific English content.

cards.title: contingency
cards.meaning: The possibility of unforeseen events or circumstances affecting an outcome.
cards.example: A humane routine accommodates contingency rather than treating every interruption as failure.
cards.conversation:
A: Why leave part of the afternoon unplanned?
B: To acknowledge contingency instead of pretending it away.
A: Does that mean abandoning plans altogether?
B: No. It means treating them as provisional responses to changing circumstances.
cards.exercise: Explain contingency in the context of a daily plan.
cards.answer: It is the possibility that circumstances or unexpected events will alter what happens.
cards.synonymNote: Uncertainty is broader; a countable contingency is a possible future circumstance.
cards.notes: Usually uncountable in this abstract sense. A contingency can also be a specific possible event for which a plan is prepared.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for contingency: path.

cards.title: instrumentalise
cards.meaning: To treat a person, activity, or experience primarily as a means to another end.
cards.example: We risk instrumentalising leisure when its only defence is improved productivity.
cards.conversation:
A: Must a hobby make us better workers?
B: Framing it that way may instrumentalise the activity.
A: Could improved productivity still be a welcome effect?
B: Certainly, provided it does not become the activity's only justification.
cards.exercise: Why might “instrumentalise leisure” be critical in tone?
cards.answer: It suggests reducing leisure to a tool for another goal and overlooking its intrinsic value.
cards.synonymNote: These capture the critical emphasis on using something for an external purpose.
cards.notes: Often critical in tone, implying that intrinsic value or agency is being overlooked. Instrumentalize is the common American spelling.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for instrumentalise: magnifier.

cards.title: make allowance for
cards.meaning: To adjust a judgement or arrangement in recognition of a relevant circumstance.
cards.example: The schedule makes allowance for uneven energy and unexpected demands.
cards.conversation:
A: Why does the plan include spare time?
B: It makes allowance for the unpredictability of ordinary life.
A: How much flexibility should a routine allow?
B: Enough to respond to circumstances without losing its guiding purpose.
cards.exercise: Rewrite using this phrase: The plan accommodates interruptions.
cards.answer: The plan makes allowance for interruptions.
cards.notes: Use make allowance for + a noun. The phrase signals accommodation, not necessarily approval of what is being accommodated.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for make allowance for: path.

cards.title: stand back from
cards.meaning: To gain perspective by temporarily distancing yourself from immediate involvement.
cards.example: It helps to stand back from the routine and ask what it serves.
cards.conversation:
A: Should I add another tracking tool?
B: First, stand back from the system and consider its purpose.
A: What might that distance reveal?
B: That a useful tool has quietly become the measure of success itself.
cards.exercise: What mental action does “stand back from” describe here?
cards.answer: Gaining perspective by temporarily stepping away from immediate involvement.
cards.notes: This use is figurative. Stand back from an argument or process to examine its assumptions and purpose.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for stand back from: path.

cards.title: the tail wagging the dog
cards.meaning: A situation in which a secondary element comes to control the larger purpose it should serve.
cards.example: When the tracker dictates the walk, the tail is wagging the dog.
cards.conversation:
A: I walked only to reach a number on my screen.
B: That sounds like the tail wagging the dog.
A: Would you stop using the tracker?
B: Perhaps, or keep it only where it supports the walk rather than directs it.
cards.exercise: Identify the “tail” and “dog” in the example.
cards.answer: The tracker is the tail; the walk and its purpose are the dog.
cards.notes: The idiom usually criticises a reversal of priorities. Explain which element is the tool and which is the purpose.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for the tail wagging the dog: compass.

cards.title: leave well enough alone
cards.meaning: To refrain from altering a situation that is already satisfactory.
cards.example: The routine was pleasant and workable, so I decided to leave well enough alone.
cards.conversation:
A: Will you redesign the schedule again?
B: No. It works for me. I will leave well enough alone.
A: How will you know when a change is needed?
B: I will reconsider when the routine stops serving the life it is meant to support.
cards.exercise: What judgement does this idiom imply?
cards.answer: Further intervention may be unnecessary or may make a satisfactory situation worse.
cards.notes: Often expresses caution that unnecessary intervention could make matters worse. It does not imply that improvement is never possible.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for leave well enough alone: compass.

cards.title: A life cannot be judged solely by the efficiency of its arrangements.
cards.meaning: The value of a life cannot be assessed only by how efficiently its activities are organised.
cards.example: A life cannot be judged solely by the efficiency of its arrangements.
cards.conversation:
A: The afternoon produced nothing measurable.
B: That does not mean it lacked value.
A: Then efficiency has no value at all?
B: That does not follow. The claim rejects it as the sole criterion.
cards.exercise: Paraphrase the sentence while preserving “solely”.
cards.answer: The efficiency of our plans cannot be the sole measure of a life’s value.
cards.notes: Solely restricts the criticism: efficiency is not excluded as a consideration, but it cannot be the only criterion.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for A life cannot be judged solely by the efficiency of its arrangements.: people.

cards.title: Some moments matter precisely because they ask for no return.
cards.meaning: Some experiences have value in themselves without needing to produce an additional benefit.
cards.example: An unhurried conversation needed no outcome. Some moments matter precisely because they ask for no return.
cards.conversation:
A: What did that conversation achieve?
B: Perhaps achievement is not the most useful question.
A: Could we value it without defending its usefulness?
B: Yes. Enjoyment or connection may be reasons enough.
cards.exercise: Explain “return” in this context.
cards.answer: A measurable benefit, result or reward expected from an experience.
cards.notes: This is an original practice reflection. Return means a benefit or payoff; precisely because makes the absence of a payoff part of the reason they matter.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for Some moments matter precisely because they ask for no return.: light.

cards.title: Were it not for…
cards.meaning: A formal inversion of If it were not for, used to imagine the absence of a present condition.
cards.example: Were it not for those unplanned conversations, the routine would feel empty.
cards.conversation:
A: Why protect time that has no fixed purpose?
B: Were it not for those open moments, my days would feel mechanical.
A: Is the sentence describing a past event?
B: No. Were it not for introduces an unreal present condition here.
cards.exercise: Rewrite with inversion: If it were not for small interruptions, I would rarely notice my neighbours.
cards.answer: Were it not for small interruptions, I would rarely notice my neighbours.
cards.notes: Use Were it not for + a noun phrase, followed by would or could + a verb. For a past counterfactual, use Had it not been for.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for Were it not for…: notebook.

cards.title: What would you keep even if it offered no measurable benefit?
cards.meaning: A question about which activities you value independently of any measurable result.
cards.example: What would you keep in your day even if it offered no measurable benefit?
cards.conversation:
A: What would you keep even if it offered no measurable benefit?
B: Looking out of the window with a cup of tea. I would rather not turn it into a project.
A: Is refusing measurement a rejection of reflection?
B: Not necessarily. We can reflect on an experience without demanding a numerical return.
cards.exercise: Respond in two sentences, distinguishing value from measurement.
cards.answer: I would keep singing while I cook. Its value lies in the enjoyment itself, whether or not I can measure a benefit.
cards.notes: Even if introduces a hypothetical concession. A thoughtful response can distinguish intrinsic value from an external justification.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for What would you keep even if it offered no measurable benefit?: dialogue.

cards.title: The unmeasured afternoon
cards.meaning: A critique of treating efficiency and measurable returns as the final authority over everyday life.
paragraphs: Optimisation promises to release us into a fuller life, yet its methods can quietly redefine what fullness means. Routines serve us best when they protect attention while leaving experiences free from the demand to produce measurable returns.

Structure can protect attention by limiting avoidable demands. Reserving an afternoon for a walk, for example, prevents work from absorbing every available hour. The arrangement is useful precisely because it creates space for experience, rather than specifying in advance what the walk must accomplish.

That space also needs protection from compulsory measurement. A walk judged only by distance or pace can become another performance test, while an unexpected conversation appears as wasted time. Making allowance for contingency lets an experience acquire value that no advance target could adequately describe.

The issue is therefore not whether routines are desirable, but what authority they should hold. Structure can secure time without dictating every use of it. An unhurried afternoon may yield no measurable return and still justify the arrangements that made it possible.
cards.exercise: How does the writer distinguish helpful structure from excessive measurement?
cards.answer: Helpful structure protects time and attention; excessive measurement dictates an experience’s value through targets and can exclude unexpected pleasures.
cards.structure: Frame a qualified thesis about routines. Develop attention-protecting structure and openness to unmeasured value with a connected example. Return to the limits of measurement.
cards.notes: Follow the main idea through two supported points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.
cards.illustrationAlt: Hand-drawn scene for The unmeasured afternoon: book.
